messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amir is a 27-year-old physical therapist, married for three years, who came to therapy at his wife’s urging after months of increasing withdrawal. He described the traumatic event that had reshaped his life: two years ago, during a late shift at the rehabilitation clinic where he worked, a male patient—a man in his forties recovering from a knee replacement—lunged from the treatment table and assaulted him. The man had been wearing a heavy, musky cologne, and as he pinned Amir down, the scent filled Amir’s nostrils while the man’s hand pressed into the surgical scar on Amir’s own lower back, a remnant of a childhood injury. The pain was sharp, specific, and Amir froze, unable to push him off until a colleague heard the struggle and intervened. The man was arrested, but for Amir, the event did not end.

In the weeks that followed, Amir found himself unable to shake the feeling that his body had been permanently marked. He had always prided himself on his physical competence—his hands were his tools, his strength his livelihood—but now he felt a deep shame about what had happened to his body. He began to avoid thinking about the assault altogether. When a memory surfaced, he would deliberately shift his attention, telling himself it had happened to someone else, a stranger in a story he had overheard. This dissociation was not a choice he made consciously; it became a reflex, a way to survive the day. Yet the avoidance did not bring peace. Instead, it left him feeling hollow, and he became certain that he would never be able to feel normal emotions again. That belief—that his emotional world was permanently broken—gnawed at him, and he started to scan his body constantly for signs of danger or injury. Every ache, every twinge in his lower back felt like a warning, a cue that he was still vulnerable, still unsafe.

The clinic became a minefield. The scent of cologne on a patient would hit him before he saw the person, and his stomach would drop. In those moments, the shame would surge—he felt ashamed of his body for having been violated, ashamed that he could not simply move on. That shame, in turn, made him hypervigilant. He became easily startled: a patient’s unexpected movement on the treatment table would make him flinch, and if someone touched him without warning, he would react with a visible alarm that embarrassed him. He noticed that his startle response was worst when he was already monitoring his body; the more he checked for pain, the more likely he was to be caught off guard by a sudden touch or a shift in the room. This created a loop he could not escape: the pain in his back would remind him of the assault, which would trigger his shame, which would heighten his vigilance, which would make him even more reactive to the next unexpected movement or scent.

Over time, Amir’s avoidance became more elaborate. He stopped working with male patients who wore cologne, requesting reassignments that his supervisor granted without question. He avoided sexual intimacy with his wife, afraid that any touch near his lower back would send him into a panic. The more he avoided, the more sensitive he became. The scent of cologne, once merely unpleasant, now felt like a direct threat, and his startle response grew so pronounced that he would jump at the sound of a door opening. He had come to believe that he could not rely on himself to stay calm, that his body was no longer under his control. That belief made him avoid even the thought of the assault, because thinking about it felt like stepping into a trap he could not escape.

What finally brought Amir to seek help was a moment at work when a colleague accidentally brushed his shoulder from behind. Amir spun around, fists raised, heart pounding, and saw the terror on the colleague’s face. He realized then that he was becoming someone he did not recognize. He is afraid that he will lose his marriage, his career, and any sense of safety in his own skin. He hopes, quietly, that therapy can help him feel like himself again—though he is not sure what that would mean anymore.
